turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the sixteenth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
A Singapore-flagged container ship is on the bottom of the Strait of Hormuz, and nobody has said they fired.
[thoughtful] Eleven days of smoke over this island. In twelve years, not one company fined.
And the luxury tap on your wall turns out to be a Hungarian cartridge in somebody else's brass.
[amused] I am going to need that one slowly, and with diagrams.
You'll get it. The spine today is the unclaimed — things that happened, to which nobody will put a name.
Lead first.
The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said on Wednesday that two Singapore-registered container ships had been struck by — their words — unknown projectiles, in the Strait of Hormuz.
Two of them?

The GFS Pride was hit on Tuesday. She caught fire and she sank. Twenty-one crew got off without injury. Her sister ship was hit the next day, took hull damage, and reached anchorage under her own propulsion.
[exhales] All of them, both ships. That's the first thing worth saying out loud.
All of them. And this is no flag-of-convenience arrangement — a Singapore company as registered owner, managed from the Emirates by a firm Reuters could not reach.
So what does the flag state say actually happened?

That's the story. The release calls the attacks unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law. Strong words — and carefully empty. No spokesperson is named. Iran is not named. Nobody is named.
[pause] For the flag state of a ship on the bottom, that is a sentence somebody built.

It is. And Tehran's account isn't a claim of responsibility at all. Tasnim, close to the Revolutionary Guards, reported a box ship exploded and sank after striking a naval mine — on what Tehran calls an unauthorised route.
Unauthorised meaning what?

The American-escorted corridor along the Omani coast, which Iran calls illegal. So: she wandered where she shouldn't have, and the sea did the rest. Then an unnamed Iranian naval officer said this on Thursday — the Strait of Hormuz is closed. If it were not closed, oil would be passing through it.
[skeptical] Is it closed?

Central Command says the opposite — that American forces and partners clearly control the strait, and helped move more than nineteen million barrels of crude through it the previous day. Al Jazeera reports two point nine million.
[laughs] Those cannot both be a day's oil through the same water.
They almost certainly aren't counting the same thing. We print both and say we can't reconcile them, because we can't.
And the sceptic?

The dissent isn't about how she sank. It's the word closed. Kpler put Gulf flows excluding Iran above eighty-one per cent of pre-war levels in September; a Vanguard analyst got to about eighty independently.
So four fifths of the traffic still moves through a strait somebody is calling shut.
Which is why closed is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence.
What would settle it?
A flag-state casualty investigation — Singapore opening the file and publishing it. Or transits back at a hundred and thirty a day.
Until then, a sunken ship with no author.
[deadpan] Welcome to the issue.
Stay on the wire. China has an airfield in Laos — its first overseas air installation.
Confirmed this week by its own defence ministry, thirty miles from Vientiane. Beijing calls it the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Centre — and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
[chuckles] An academy.

It says it will help Laos train its pilots and is not directed against any third party. Imagery from September shows a runway of roughly six thousand five hundred feet, and room to lengthen it by three thousand more.
Which would take what?
Analysts say bombers. And Laos did not respond. Neither did Vietnam, Cambodia or Myanmar.
[pause] An academy. And nobody's claiming this one either. One more unclaimed thing — the drones.

Ukrainian Starshield terminals began dropping connection above a speed threshold, which crippled mid-range strike drones. Elon Musk says the systems are owned and controlled by the United States government. Officials called it a technical malfunction. The White House denied any role. The Pentagon has not explained.
[scoffs] A cap that nobody imposed.
A serving soldier said it came without warning and cost tens of millions of dollars. A senator wants an inquiry into either an unacceptable error — or a conscious decision to clear the field.
That's the spine four times, and we're on page four.
Money. The Kospi closed down seven point five seven per cent on Thursday, after a circuit breaker halted trading for twenty minutes.
[gasps] Twenty minutes.
Samsung fell nine and a half per cent, SK hynix eleven, and foreigners sold a net three point six trillion won.
Why?

It's upstream, and it's the war. September American consumer prices rose three point seven per cent, petrol up thirty-four on the year. The White House adviser Kevin Hassett conceded it: the energy shock is really the headline story today.
So the inflation came out of the strait. And then?
Thursday the bond market blinked. The ten-year fell eleven basis points, and the odds of a Federal Reserve hike this month dropped to twenty-five per cent, from thirty-seven.
Thirty-seven to twenty-five in a day?
[wry] A market changing its mind twice in forty-eight hours is not a market forming a view.
What's the tell for you?

TSMC. A record quarter, margins above its own guidance — and the index it sits in fell three point four per cent. When earnings that good are marked down that hard, the market isn't disputing them. It's repricing what a future dollar of them is worth.
And the sensible portfolio?

The all-world index is flat on the week and up seventeen per cent over a year. Global bonds finally helped, up half a per cent on a day equities broke. Hold that lightly — their one-year return is still negative. They hedged Thursday. They have not hedged the year.
Singapore held, though.

The Straits Times Index fell a third of a per cent on a day Korea fell seven and a half — resilience, or only composition. Our central bank held policy on Wednesday while saying the risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. A bank that holds while saying that is not relaxed.
Home, then. The air.
At five this morning the National Environment Agency's own machine feed read two hundred and nineteen in central Singapore.
Two hundred and nineteen.
It crossed the two hundred band in the dark.
And five days ago, on this show, you said the opposite.
I did. We printed that it had peaked at one hundred and sixty-eight and the published rung had never been reached. It has now, and we say so on page five.
So what does crossing it trigger?

That's the thing — crossing it does not start a case. The Prime Minister wrote on Thursday night that Singapore is working out which companies are responsible. The Act has stood since two thousand and fourteen: a hundred thousand dollars a day, to a two million cap.
And in twelve years?
No company has been fined or sued under it. Not one.
[sighs] Is that timidity?

That's the usual reading. The harder one is evidentiary — Singapore must show, to a court's standard, that a named company's concession produced smoke that crossed a border. From satellite hotspots. Against companies under no obligation to help.
And Greenpeace?
Greenpeace has named concessions containing smoke sources — and carefully says the findings don't establish that those companies lit fires. That caution is the whole problem in one clause.
And the schools?
The Education Minister wrote on the tenth that they would close, and examinations be postponed, only above three hundred. The index stood at one hundred and sixty-eight when he wrote it.
And we're at two nineteen.
The forum got there before the commentary did. One user: talk so big, but two eighty can't even forecast — three hundred then how?
[laughs] That's a fair question in nine words.

Meanwhile a twelve-year-old is sitting national papers in an air-purified hall. The exemption from outdoor activity is a right, not a favour, and a child who is unwell can apply for Special Consideration. That's what a parent can act on.
Technology. Who is paying for the fabs?

Japan. GlobalFoundries will operate two new fabs at its campus in Malta, New York, under an initiative the release describes in Japan's own words — up to twenty-one billion US dollars. Its own fees are not disclosed.
[curious] So who owns it?
Count the flags on one building. A foreign treasury pays. An American company whose majority holder is an Abu Dhabi fund operates it. Washington takes four per cent. It opens in twenty twenty-nine.
Home lab. Something small and strange.
NVIDIA released a model that fits seventy-four billion parameters into twenty-four gigabytes, by quantising its expert weights to about two bits each.
[excited] Seventy-four billion on a desktop card. That is genuinely impressive engineering.

The engineering is. The speed isn't — on NVIDIA's own benchmark it runs at eighty-four tokens a second, against a hundred and fifty for a model a third its size. It wins ten of thirteen benchmarks and loses both hallucination metrics.
So it answers more and gets more of them wrong.
An honest trade, and NVIDIA published both halves. [deadpan] Across five separate submissions in its first day, it drew two comments on Hacker News.
[laughs] Two.

Gear. Microsoft began shipping the Surface Laptop Ultra on Wednesday at two thousand five hundred and ninety-nine US dollars. Its Singapore site lists neither it nor the companion workstation; the Singapore address resolves to the American page.
Third week running you've found that hole.
Third week. And the counter-example lands the same day — Apple opens pre-orders here at eight tonight, and Singapore is in the first wave.
[wry] So it isn't that we're small. Somebody decided.

And the sceptic is worse than the pricing. One reviewer's unit powered itself off three times in four attempts under a heavy solve, each within sixteen seconds. No crash dump, no fatal error, no thermal event — and heat is ruled out: the same machine held ninety-eight degrees for half an hour without faulting.
[gasps] It turned itself off, and nobody has said why. Right. The Atelier. Explain my tap to me.

Start with the brass, because solid brass is not one thing. The default hot-forging tap brass is disqualified by its own maker's datasheet in a sentence: the high lead content means it cannot be used in contact with drinking water.
[laughs] Well, that is a sentence. And the part that actually breaks?

The cartridge. Kerox, of Sóskút in Hungary, has sold five hundred and forty million. And an American luxury marque ships a genuine spare whose distributor lists it as — I'm quoting — cartridge assembly, Kerox K forty-five.
So the luxury spare is the Hungarian part in a different box.
And Kerox buys in too — its own quality page admits outsourced metal components. The vertical integration everyone imagines exists nowhere in this category.
Then where is the theatre?

The list price, and the finish. At one German dealer this week a luxury line sat at minus forty-seven per cent — prices routinely halved are not prices. And Axor's V one forty is nine hundred and fifty-nine euros plain, twelve hundred and twenty-eight in gold.
Two hundred and sixty-eight euros for the colour.

For the colour. And Singapore ends the argument by law — since two thousand and nineteen only two-tick fittings may be installed, which caps a shower mixer at seven litres a minute. The flow is identical whatever you spend.
[thoughtful] Then what does the money buy?
A thicker machined body, a better finish, a lead time and a spares chain. Not a longer-lived cartridge. The cartridge that fails is the same one.
That is the most useful thing anyone has ever told me about a tap. Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week.
[laughs] It never gets old. What are we doing?
Caving. Sport caving — unlit, unpaved, unguided. Not the cave with handrails and a guide.
How big is it?
Eight and a half thousand members in America, a hundred and fifty-four clubs in Britain. The forum that functions as the hobby's capital carries four hundred and twenty-six thousand messages.
And the characteristic emergency? I assume a fall.
That's what everyone assumes, and it isn't. Across five years the leading cause is being lost or overdue — forty-three against twelve for falls — and the leading injury is hypothermia.
[curious] So it's a cold, lost party, not a dramatic drop.
Last year in the British Isles: twenty-five incidents, forty people assisted, one underground fatality, no helicopter evacuation. Fifteen of the twenty-five ended with nobody hurt.
And the one death?
Stated exactly as the report states it. A party heard a bang and the rope became taut. The cause was unclear, the coroner awaited. They published that rather than smooth it.
Who does the rescuing?
Volunteers. Sixteen teams in Britain gave five thousand five hundred and seventy unpaid hours last year.
[exhales] Five and a half thousand hours. Unpaid.
And the economics are strange. Membership is about thirty-two pounds a year and carries twenty million pounds of public liability indemnity.
Twenty million? For crawling into a hole?
The policy exists chiefly to reassure the farmer whose field the cave runs under. Caving's core financial instrument is a landowner-relations product.
[laughs] That's the best sentence of the issue.

And the card is functionally a passport. Mulu, in Sarawak, will sell you a night at the mouth of the largest cave chamber on earth for three hundred and fifteen ringgit — but only if you satisfy the park manager in writing. The alternative is Son Doong, three thousand US dollars for six days, booked out two years.
And how does a person get in?

Getting in is a university club, a taster day, or simply asking. The advice on the British forum is unanimous and oddly tender — one poster says it's worth contacting the local clubs to see if they can take you under their wing.
[warmly] Under their wing.

Another: I joined a club aged sixteen and it was one of the best things I ever did. But the northern training council listed fifteen workshops this quarter. Eleven are full, and it warns it may not keep offering training after December.
Demand outstripping volunteers. Again. All right — the gear.

A complete beginner's outfit is about three hundred pounds. The vertical hardware, bought once, is another three to four hundred. Then the lamp. A Scurion fifteen hundred, made in Switzerland, is seven hundred and twenty-six pounds.
[gasps] The lamp costs more than everything else?

More than the clothing, the helmet, the boots and the rope work combined. And the first contest is the number — Scurion's own site rates it at thirteen hundred lumens, its British dealer at sixteen hundred.
Someone's lying.

Neither is. Scurion uses the industry standard, which is more honest and lower; virtually every other manufacturer quotes emitter lumens. One measures light leaving the lamp, the other light leaving the diode.
[chuckles] Three hundred lumens between a product and itself.

But the best part of this hobby is the survey instruments — the thing cavers build for each other. In twelve months the American market leader stopped production, the Shetland maker suspended his, and a Chinese entrant arrived at five hundred and sixty euros.
The market leader stopped — bankruptcy?
Confirmed by absence. Its American retailer's entire survey collection now holds no instrument at all. Waterproof paper and books.
And the Shetland one?

He open-sourced the whole project, and his shop explains he has suspended orders to build a successor. He wrote: it's just me doing this. He also notes a twenty-eight pound American tariff must be paid per device, by PayPal.
[sighs] That's the entire global trading system landing on one man's kitchen table.

And the newest maker developed his in public, and let the price creep in public too — four hundred and fifty pounds last September, now five hundred and twenty-five. Then he announced his own mistake: the wrong regulator for the laser. He told the people who had already bought one.
[warmly] That is the opposite of everything else in this issue.

Exactly the opposite, and that's why it's in it. One last detail — the instruments talk to a phone, and the phones are deliberately terrible. One caver uses a Galaxy Note he bought for twenty pounds, because the battery is replaceable. Another uses a seventy-pound Motorola, because you can always drop it down a tight rift and never see it again.
[laughs] Perfect. Genuinely perfect.
Culture. Fontaines D.C. released their fifth album today — and my problem isn't the record, it's the clock. The five-star review was published on Monday. Four days early.
And by release day?

A score of eighty-four across fourteen reviews was circulating on Thursday — a consensus published before the public could hear the thing being scored. And we couldn't check it: the aggregator refused us, so it's printed as unverified.
The body. There's a study I want to be annoyed about.

Three thousand British civil servants, followed eighteen years. Meeting the physical-activity guideline, on its own, did almost nothing to cognitive-impairment risk — twenty-four point nine per cent against a natural course of twenty-five and a half.
[sighs] So exercise doesn't work.

That's the headline I'd resist. Stack the behaviours and it changes: activity with diet, with not smoking, and with all four vascular targets gives a risk ratio of nought point eight six. It works in company.
And the honest caveat?

Self-report, in an unusually healthy cohort, with impairment defined statistically rather than clinically. A null produced that way is the likeliest kind to be measurement error. One thing you can act on — a smartwatch estimate of your aerobic capacity flatters the unfit by up to sixteen per cent.
[thoughtful] Resist the headline in both directions. Objects — something sold out before I finished reading about it.

A hundred and twenty-five watches, from a Malaysian maker and a Geneva collaborator, went on sale Wednesday at seven thousand two hundred and fifty Swiss francs. The maker's page says sold out, and that it will not be produced again — then offers a waitlist and quotes eight to twelve weeks.
The page contradicts itself.

So we print the contradiction rather than a sell-out time. The interesting part is the dial: a lacquered base under three rotating sapphire discs, on twenty-four-hour, twelve-hour and sixty-minute cycles, so the pattern reorganises itself continuously.
And the diary?
Our local arts centre is running twenty-nine free shows this month, every one free. Though of twenty-three listings in this agenda, ten publish no price at all at the primary source.
[skeptical] Ten of twenty-three won't tell you what it costs. And food?

And a gelato kiosk from Telok Ayer has reopened on Amoy Street as a sit-down café built as a hanok, a Korean house — do-it-yourself affogato at ten dollars, twelve combinations. Though three of this week's five openings have one review each, from the same outlet.
The Undercurrent. Taiwan.

[thoughtful] On the thirtieth of July, Taiwan's Executive Yuan recognised the Siraya as the island's seventeenth Indigenous people — the first plains group ever admitted, after thirty years of campaigning and a unanimous Constitutional Court judgment.
And then what happened?
Registration opened in August. By the end of September, twelve thousand one hundred and seventy-eight had applied. One thousand three hundred and thirty-six had completed registration.
Out of how many?
The Council projected about fifty thousand in the first year. Its own estimate of how many people in Taiwan carry plains-Indigenous ancestry is nine hundred and eighty thousand.
[pause] Nine hundred and eighty thousand, and one thousand three hundred.

The gap isn't indifference. It's a price signal, and three things set the price. First, the evidence test is a colonial archive — the Act accepts Japanese-era household records as proof of membership.
Meaning what, in practice?

Finding a register in which a Japanese census-taker wrote the character shú — cooked — beside a great-grandmother's name. You are Indigenous in twenty twenty-six if a colonial clerk thought your ancestors had assimilated in nineteen thirty-five.
[exhales] That's a hell of a sentence.

Second, recognition arrived without rights. Three statutes apply directly; a hundred and eighteen laws are queued for amendment; and the Act instructs the government merely to consider legislating within three years. Third, the six reserved seats are in the Constitution.
Has Taiwan run this experiment before?

Twice — and used the result as proof the people did not exist. In the nineteen fifties and sixties it opened brief windows to register. Almost nobody did: stigma was heavy, notification poor. Officials treated that as the Siraya voluntarily relinquishing their status, and it stood for half a century.
And a closer precedent?

In two thousand and seven Taiwan recognised the Sakizaya. About twenty thousand people had signed in support of that recognition. Nineteen years on, the registered count stands at one thousand two hundred and thirty-seven.
[pause] And the Siraya's thirteen hundred is already tracking it.
Almost exactly. Taiwan has already learned what a recognised people with few attached rights registers at.
Is there an honest objection from inside?

Two, and both are serious. From the recognised sixteen: the Indigenous population is a fixed pool — reserved land, quotas, scholarships, seats. Adding a million divides it. Not bigotry; arithmetic. And from the plains side, that recognition is demotion — a youth alliance calls the Act one people, three systems.
Siblings in one household with different rights.

Depending on whether an ancestor once filled in a form. The register runs to twenty thirty-one, so two months is nothing, and that objection deserves its hearing. But nineteen years of Sakizaya is not lag.
[pause] So what's the honest conclusion?

That Taiwan built a two-tier structure without the uptake, because it built it without the entitlements. The register is the receipt. Twelve thousand thought the offer was worth a form. One thousand three hundred completed it.
[thoughtful] And that's the spine again — a people recognised on terms almost nobody collected, and nobody made to answer for it.
Which is why the quote on page two is a standard and not a joke. Kennedy used the old line about a hundred fathers on the day he took sole responsibility for a failure that had several.
So the question isn't who's hiding.

Mostly that's obvious. The question is what it costs a system to make someone sign. Sixteen volunteer rescue teams gave five thousand five hundred and seventy unpaid hours last year, and logged every incident — including their one death — in a public document that says plainly where the cause is unknown.
[warmly] Nobody made them.
Nobody made them. That's what putting your name to something looks like when you've decided to.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
